Carbon. The foundation of all known organic life on Earth. This nonmetallic element can bond with itself and an enormous variety of other elements in stable covalent connections, giving rise to essentially infinite organic compounds. In its pure state, carbon takes on several distinct forms called allotropes, each with wildly different physical properties. Diamond, for instance, is tetrahedral and exceptionally hard because each carbon atom is sp3 hybridized. Graphite, on the other hand, is soft and slippery because it's layered—its sp2 hybridized sheets are held together only by weak van der Waals forces. Then there are fullerenes and nanotubes: closed cage structures like the soccer-ball-shaped buckminsterfullerene, or C60, along with cylindrical tubes that have extraordinary tensile strength. Carbon also exists in amorphous forms—charcoal, coal, and carbon black—which lack any long-range crystal structure.

The element's most defining characteristic is catenation: its ability to form long chains and rings through carbon-carbon bonds, and this catenation is what makes organic chemistry possible. With four valence electrons, carbon can form four covalent bonds arranged in tetrahedral, planar, or linear geometry. Scientists use carbon-14, one of its isotopes, for radiocarbon dating; carbon-14 has a half-life of roughly five thousand seven hundred thirty years. Carbon-12, meanwhile, serves as the standard for atomic mass itself—it's defined as exactly twelve daltons. In stars, carbon-12 forms through the triple-alpha process, where three helium-4 nuclei fuse together inside red giants. Carbon and nitrogen work together in the CNO cycle, catalyzing hydrogen fusion in the most massive stars. Carbon and oxygen form carbon dioxide, which is critical to photosynthesis and the carbon cycle itself. Carbon, nitrogen, and hydrogen make up organic reactions and functional groups, the structural parts of molecules that determine how they behave chemically. In any geology class or chemistry lab, you'll find that carbon forms diamond, that spectacular sp3 allotrope used as both a gemstone and an industrial abrasive.
